purpose: Raw material for the ~8 s cold open of the Satchel launch film: real headlines and posts about the problems Satchel answers. Raw captures are UNBLURRED; apply the blur list in each item before use.

capture.tool: Playwright Chromium (apps/web @playwright/test), deviceScaleFactor 2, timezone UTC, locale en-US, one browser at a time
capture.xPosts: Public embed https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=<ID>&theme=<light|dark>&dnt=true&lang=en (no login). Element screenshot of the post card, transparent rounded corners. Times on cards are UTC.
capture.pages: Viewport 1280 CSS px (PNG 2560 px wide). Cookie/consent dialogs, newsletter pop-ups and ad slots hidden with CSS or removed before capture; requests to common ad/video-ad domains blocked. No words, numbers or layout of the article were edited.
blockedByBotCheck: bleepingcomputer.com (Cloudflare check): Trust Wallet, Ledger implant, snail-mail letters, $494M drainers articles
capture.notBypassed: Pages behind a bot check were skipped, not circumvented.

items.text:
⚠️ Reminder that if you ever stored your private keys or seed phrases in LastPass prior to 2023, your funds might be at risk. We've seen 15+ cases of potential LastPass-related hacks TODAY

Move your assets before hackers move them for you. For more information, keep reading🧵
items.mapsTo: A seed phrase copied years ago can still empty a wallet today. Satchel: its BTC/ETH/SOL addresses have no seed phrase, so there is nothing to copy or leak.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED as SEAL's own post (primary). The '15+ cases' count is SEAL's claim, not independently checked.

items.text: Feds Link $150M Cyberheist to 2022 LastPass Hacks
items.mapsTo: Seed phrases kept in a password manager were stolen in 2022 and used to drain wallets in 2024. Satchel: no seed phrase to store.
items.factCheck: REPORTED (Krebs quoting a federal seizure filing: ~$24M seized from a $150M theft on 2024-01-30; victims had stored seed phrases in LastPass Secure Notes). LastPass says it has seen no conclusive evidence of the link.
items.people: Header photo of Brian Krebs (journalist, public figure). Site ad hidden at capture.

items.text: 🔒 If you have enabled iCloud backup for app data, this will include your password-encrypted MetaMask vault. If your password isn’t strong enough, and someone phishes your iCloud credentials, this can mean stolen funds. (Read on 👇) 1/3
items.mapsTo: Wallet backups end up in the cloud and get phished. Satchel: nothing to back up for the chain addresses.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary post). The triggering ~$650K loss is REPORTED (Decrypt, The Block, AppleInsider, Apr 2022).

items.text:
This exploit was isolated to one wallet on Solana, and hardware wallets used by Slope remain secure.

While the details of exactly how this occurred are still under investigation, but private key information was inadvertently transmitted to an application monitoring service.  2/3
items.captureNote: Captured with hideThread=true: shows post 2/3 only ('Replying to @SolanaStatus').
items.mapsTo: A wallet app leaked private keys to a logging service and thousands of wallets were drained. Satchel: no private key or seed phrase on the user's device for the chain addresses.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary post). Scale is REPORTED and varies: 'almost 8,000 wallets' (The Block, 2022-08-03); $4M-$8M in other outlets.

items.text: Kaspersky discovers new crypto-stealing Trojan in AppStore and Google Play
items.mapsTo: Malware reads screenshots of recovery phrases from phone galleries (SparkCat). Satchel: no recovery phrase to photograph.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary): 'first known instance of optical recognition-based malware appearing in AppStore'; Google Play apps 'downloaded over 242,000 times'; it steals 'screenshots containing cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases'.

We’ve confirmed that approximately $7M has been impacted and we will ensure all affected users are refunded.

Supporting affected users is our top priority, and we are actively finalizing the process to refund the Show more

We’ve identified a security incident affecting Trust Wallet Browser Extension version 2.68 only. Users with Browser Extension 2.68 should disable and upgrade to 2.69.

items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary: Trust Wallet's own '$7M'). Seed-phrase exfiltration is REPORTED (SlowMist analysis, quoted by The Hacker News).

items.mapsTo: Same incident as T1-06, as a news headline.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED ($7M per Trust Wallet's post; SlowMist: 'Once decrypted, the mnemonic phrase is sent to the attacker's server').
items.people: Journalist byline only. Site ads hidden at capture.

items.text: Ledger details LTE-enabled spy implants in wallets sold by CryptoBilis
items.mapsTo: Hardware wallets bought from a reseller came with an implant that copied the 24-word phrase during setup: someone else had the keys from day one. Satchel: no phrase is ever shown, so there is nothing to capture.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED that Ledger Donjon described the implant (decodes the 24 words shown during setup, sends them over LTE via eSIM). Loss totals are UNVERIFIED ('could exceed $86 million' per investigator Specter; $103M per Yfarmx; Ledger hasn't confirmed a total). Do not show a dollar figure for this case.
items.brandNote: Ledger-related; use at most one Ledger item in the cut.

items.text:
Update from Ledger Donjon on the CryptoBilis investigation 🔽

@DonjonLedger is investigating Ledger signers sold by CryptoBilis, a reseller in Southeast Asia, that contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Ledger confirmed this on October 10th for one affected user's signer. Show more
items.mapsTo: Primary statement for T1-08.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary).

items.text:
Breaking: New scam meta launched. Now they’re sending physical letters to the @Ledger addresses database leak requesting an ‘upgrade’ due to a security risk.

Be very cautious and warn any friends or family that you know is in crypto and is not that savvy.
items.mapsTo: A paper letter, styled as Ledger, asks owners to scan a QR code and enter their recovery phrase. Satchel: there is no recovery phrase to phish for the chain addresses.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED: Ledger replied 'You are correct, this is a scam.' (https://x.com/Ledger/status/1917209656973213746, 2025-04-29); The Block reported it on 2025-04-30.
items.people: Individual (crypto trader/influencer with a verified account; semi-public). Two photos of the letter held in his hand.

blur: avatar, display name and @handle (individual) unless you treat him as a public figure
the QR code on the letter (it pointed to a live phishing site)
privacy.notes: Name and reference number on the letter were already redacted by the poster.

items.text: Crypto phishers are sending letters to Trezor, Ledger users again
items.mapsTo: Physical letters with QR codes lead to fake setup pages that ask for the recovery phrase.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (Cointelegraph: QR code leads to a fake site where users are tricked into 'entering their wallet recovery phrases').
items.brandNote: Names two wallet brands (as victims' vendors).

items.text: Hacker steals $282 million crypto from a victim in social-engineering attack
items.mapsTo: One person tricked out of a hardware wallet's secret: $282M gone.
items.factCheck: REPORTED ($282M in BTC and LTC per investigator ZachXBT, theft on 2026-01-10). That the victim revealed the seed phrase is UNVERIFIED (other outlets say so; CoinDesk only says 'social-engineering attack').
items.people: Stock photo (Unsplash). Black box at right is a blocked video player.

items.text:
🚨 ALERT: A victim lost $908,551 due to a phishing approval signed 458 days ago.
🔐 REMINDER: Regularly review and revoke old approvals - your wallet security matters! 💰
items.mapsTo: The film's central problem in one line: an authorization signed 458 days earlier emptied the wallet. Satchel refuses token approvals and permits, records every signature before it is made, and the buyer's browser checks that none can still move coins.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary post); Cointelegraph (2025-08-03) independently reports '$908,551 ... 458 days after unknowingly signing a malicious approval transaction' from on-chain data. On-chain transactions not checked by us.

blur: victim wallet address fragments in the attached Etherscan screenshot (e.g. 0x6c0eB6ef...9Ffb8d8aF, ...9d7c7AF129aE9D1B5E3e9Ffb8d8aF)
privacy.notes: Note: it was an on-chain approval, not an off-chain signature; say 'approval', not 'signature', in captions.

items.text: Crypto victim loses $908K in sophisticated phishing attack
items.mapsTo: Same as T2-01, as a headline with '$908K' artwork.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (see T2-01). Subhead: 'A victim lost $908,551 in a crypto phishing scam 15 months after signing a malicious approval transaction.'

items.text: Hackers Exploit Bug to "Steal" $1 Million in NFTs from OpenSea Users
items.keyLine: Those old listings are now being used to purchase NFTs at prices chosen by the seller in the past.
items.mapsTo: Old signed listings were filled long after the owners moved on: a signature outlived the moment it was made. Satchel: signing pauses while listed and the buyer checks every old signature is used up or expired.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary analysis): 'NFTs with a market value of $1.1 million have been purchased in this way'; Bored Ape #9991 bought for 0.77 ETH (~$1,800) and resold for 84.2 ETH (~$196,000).
items.people: Lead image is an OpenSea activity table with marketplace usernames.

items.mapsTo: Same incident as T2-03: old listings bought at old prices.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED via Elliptic (T2-03). OpenSea later refunded about 750 ETH (~$1.8M) (REPORTED, Decrypt).
items.people: Journalist avatar; lead image is Bored Ape #9991 (credited 'Image: Yuga Labs').

items.text: It appears that @opensea has a front-end issue and the exploiter gained about 332 Ether
items.mapsTo: Same incident, first alert.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED as PeckShield's claim (primary); 332 ETH not checked on-chain by us.

items.text: As far as we can tell, this is a phishing attack. We don’t believe it’s connected to the OpenSea website. It appears 32 users thus far have signed a malicious payload from an attacker, and some of their NFTs were stolen.
items.parent: I know you’re all worried. We’re running an all hands on deck investigation, but I want to take a minute to share the facts as I see them:
items.mapsTo: Users signed an off-chain payload that let an attacker take their NFTs. Satchel: it signs only readable requests (no raw hashes, no permits/approvals).
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary post, 2022-02-20). OpenSea later revised the count to 17 affected users (REPORTED, CoinDesk 2022-02-21); losses ~$1.7M (Engadget, T2-08).
items.people: Public figure (CEO); avatar is an NFT image.

items.text: OpenSea users lose hundreds of NFTs in likely phishing attack
items.subhead: The damage is estimated at $1.7 million.
items.mapsTo: Same incident as T2-07, mainstream tech outlet.
items.factCheck: REPORTED (Engadget citing Molly White's estimate: 641 ETH, ~$1.7M at the time).
items.people: Lead photo credited 'JUSTIN TALLIS via Getty Images' (shows NFT artworks).

privacy.notes: Getty photo: crop to the headline block unless licensed.

items.text: Bybit ETH multisig cold wallet just made a transfer to our warm wallet about 1 hr ago. It appears that this specific transaction was musked, all the signers saw the musked UI which showed the correct address and the URL was from @safe . However the signing message was to change Show more
items.captureNote: Embed truncates with 'Show more'; 'musked' is the original spelling (= masked). Do not correct it.
items.mapsTo: Every signer approved a transaction they could not read: the screen showed one thing, the signature did another. Satchel: it refuses blind signing and anything it cannot parse.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary post); amount and attribution VERIFIED by FBI PSA I-022625-PSA (T2-11).

blur: tx hash fragment 0xb61413c495... in the Etherscan card (public exchange incident), optional
privacy.notes: Do not imply Satchel would have prevented Bybit (an exchange multisig); use it only as 'signers could not read what they signed'.

items.text:
While EIP-7702 brings new convenience, it also introduces new risks

Our Research team found that over 97% of all EIP-7702 delegations were authorized to multiple contracts using the same exact code. These are sweepers, used to automatically drain incoming ETH from compromised Show more
items.mapsTo: EIP-7702 delegations were overwhelmingly sweepers draining wallets whose keys had leaked. Satchel refuses EIP-7702 authorizations and has no key to leak.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED as Wintermute's claim (primary). The Block (2025-06-01) reported 'over 80%'; the sweepers target already-compromised keys, so do not caption it as '97% of users were robbed'.

items.text: WazirX Loses $230 Million in Suspected DPRK Hack
items.subhead: WazirX lost funds exceeding $230 million in yesterday's attack, which Elliptic has said is linked to North Korea-based hackers.
items.mapsTo: Another multisig whose signers approved what the screen did not show (WazirX: 'a discrepancy between the data displayed on Liminal's interface and the transaction's actual contents').
items.factCheck: REPORTED; the cause is disputed (Liminal blames compromised WazirX devices). Elliptic estimate ~$235M.

items.text: Your keys, his coins — Cryptopia employee admits to stealing $172K in crypto
items.mapsTo: Keys copied while someone had access were used after they left. A copied secret survives every handover. Satchel: there is no secret to copy; whoever holds the NFT holds the wallet.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED in Cointelegraph's report of his guilty plea: he 'made his own copy of the information on a USB flash drive'; theft of 'roughly $172,000'. Other outlets give $170K-$177K.
items.people: Illustration; journalist avatars. The employee is not named in the capture.

items.text: Miami man arrested in theft of $1.9M in Bitcoin from former employer, cops say
items.keyLine: The wallet contained a "seed phrase" and the only people who had it were the victim and Castro
items.mapsTo: Two people knew one seed phrase; the theft went unnoticed for years. Satchel: handing over the NFT hands over control, with nothing left behind.
items.factCheck: REPORTED allegation (arrest report, May 2026); no conviction known. Say 'police say'.
items.people: PRIVATE INDIVIDUAL: the accused is named in the subhead.

blur: accused's full name in the subhead (and anywhere else)
privacy.notes: Allegation only; never present as proven.

items.text: Case study: fake hardware cryptowallet
items.subhead: Full review of a fake cryptowallet incident. It looks and feels like a Trezor wallet, but puts all your crypto-investments into the hands of criminals.
items.mapsTo: A second-hand 'hardware wallet' came with a seed phrase the sellers already knew. Buying a wallet means trusting whoever touched it before you. Satchel: the buyer's browser checks the history before Buy turns on.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (Kaspersky blog: 'the randomly generated seed phrase was replaced with one of 20 pre-generated seed phrases saved in the hacked firmware'; press release: 1.33 BTC, ~$29,585 stolen).

privacy.notes: Counterfeit device, not a Trezor flaw; brand appears in the subhead.

items.text: Scam Sniffer 2024: Web3 Phishing Attacks – Wallet Drainers Drain $494 Million
items.figureText: Crypto Phishing Report / Annual Report 2024 by ScamSniffer / $494M+ TOTAL LOSS (up 67%) / 332K+ VICTIMS (up 3.7%) / $55.4M LARGEST SINGLE LOSS (up 130%) / 30 LARGE LOSS CASES (up 56%)
items.mapsTo: Wallet drainers (malicious signatures) took about half a billion dollars in one year.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary): 'approximately $494 million in losses', '332,000 addresses'; text gives the largest theft as $55.48M (infographic rounds to $55.4M). Permit was 56.7% of large-case losses.

items.text: Scam Sniffer 2025: Crypto Phishing Losses Fall 83% to $84 Million
items.figureText: Year-over-Year Comparison / Signature Phishing Losses | 2023 - 2025 (total loss $295M / $494M / $84M; victims 324K / 332K / 106K; largest single theft $24.1M / $55.5M / $6.5M; large cases 13 / 30 / 11)
items.mapsTo: Signature phishing over three years; 2025's largest single theft was one Permit signature.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary): '$83.85M across 106,106 victims'; 'Largest single theft: $6.5M via Permit signature (September)'; 'Permit/Permit2 signatures accounted for 38% of large-case losses'. Losses FELL in 2025, so don't use this headline to imply growth.

items.text: North Korea Drives Record $2 Billion Crypto Theft Year, Pushing All-Time Total to $6.75 Billion
items.keyLine: Individual wallet compromises surged to 158,000 incidents affecting 80,000 unique victims in 2025, though total value stolen ($713M) decreased from 2024.
items.mapsTo: Personal wallets are where thefts multiply: 158,000 incidents in 2025.
items.factCheck: VERIFIED (primary): 'over $3.4 billion in theft from January through early December 2025'; 158,000 incidents; at least 80,000 victims; $713M from individuals (down from $1.5B in 2024).

privacy.notes: The TL;DR crop also shows North Korea bullets; crop to the 158,000 bullet.

That private key or seed phrase is all that is standing between you and someone trying to take your money.
